title: Romans
intro: 25 days through Paul's letter to the Romans, one passage at a time.

posts.caption: Romans is a letter from Paul to the Christians in Rome, commonly dated around AD 57, written to a church he had not founded or yet visited. This verse states its theme: the good news about Jesus is God's power to save everyone who believes, Jew first and non-Jew too. "Greek" here stands for all non-Jews. Starting today, 25 days through Romans, one passage at a time.

Paul gives the reason the gospel saves: it reveals the righteousness of God, which "comes by faith from start to finish." Readers explain "the righteousness of God" as God's own faithfulness, as the right standing God gives, or as both. Paul backs it with the prophet Habakkuk. Martin Luther wrote that grasping this verse made him feel born again, and it became central to the Protestant Reformation; John Wesley felt his heart "strangely warmed" hearing Luther's preface to Romans read aloud.

Paul begins his argument that all people, Jews and non-Jews alike, have fallen short of what God asks. He starts with non-Jews: God, he says, can be known through creation itself. Theologians call this "natural" or "general" revelation, the idea that the world points to its maker. Psalm 19 expresses something similar: "The heavens declare the glory of God."

Paul now turns to anyone who condemns others while doing the same things. A few verses later he sums up his point: "God does not show favoritism." Here he describes God's kindness and patience as giving people time; in Paul's framing, that patience is meant to lead to repentance, a change of heart and direction.

The center of Paul's argument so far: Jews and non-Jews stand in the same place, since all have fallen short, and all can be set right with God the same way, as a free gift. "Justified" is a legal term meaning declared in the right, like a verdict of acquittal; whether it also means being made righteous was a key debate of the Reformation. "Grace" (charis) means a gift freely given, and "redemption" was the word for buying back a slave or a captive.

Paul draws his conclusion: a person is put right with God by faith, apart from "works of the law," usually understood as keeping the Law of Moses. Luther's German Bible read "by faith alone," adding a word not in the Greek, and "faith alone" became a Protestant watchword. Catholic teaching also calls justification God's free gift, but sees saving faith as faith working through love. In 1999, Catholic and Lutheran leaders signed a joint declaration agreeing on basic truths of justification.

Paul turns to Abraham, the ancestor of the Jewish people, quoting Genesis 15:6. His point is that Abraham was counted righteous for trusting God before he was circumcised, so he can be the "father" of believing Jews and non-Jews alike. "Credited" is an accounting word, like a sum entered into someone's account.

Paul has just said that someone might, rarely, be willing to die for a good person. His point is that the love he describes came first, before anyone deserved it. Later in chapter 5, Paul contrasts Adam, whose disobedience brought sin and death into the world, with Christ, whose obedience brings life.

Paul answers an objection: if grace is free, why not keep sinning? His reply uses everyday Roman images of slavery and pay. "Wages" (opsonia) often meant a soldier's pay or rations, earned and owed. The contrast is deliberate: sin pays out what is earned, while eternal life is a gift (charisma), something no one earns.

Paul describes a divided self: knowing what is good and not doing it. Readers have long debated who this "I" is. Augustine first read it as a person living under the law before faith, but later concluded it describes the ongoing struggle of believers, a view Luther and Calvin shared. Many modern scholars see the "I" as a figure of speech for humanity, or Israel, under the law.

Chapter 8 is often called one of the high points of Paul's letters, and it opens by answering the struggle of chapter 7: for those united with Christ, there is no guilty verdict left to fear. "Condemnation" is a courtroom word for a guilty verdict and its penalty. Paul goes on to describe life shaped by God's Spirit: the Greek word pneuma appears only a handful of times earlier in Romans, but around twenty times in this chapter alone.

A verse many people turn to in hard times. Paul isn't saying everything that happens is good, but that God works through all of it, even suffering, toward good for those who love him. Ancient manuscripts and translations differ slightly here: some read "all things work together for good," others "God works all things together for good." The next verse describes that good as being shaped into the likeness of Christ.

The climax of chapter 8. Paul lists everything he can think of, from death and life to angels and "principalities," a word for ruling powers, human or spiritual. Some scholars think "height" and "depth" were terms from ancient astrology for the sky above and below the horizon. His conclusion: nothing in all creation can separate believers from God's love.

In chapters 9 to 11, Paul wrestles with a hard question: why had most of his fellow Jews not accepted Jesus as Messiah? He imagines an objector asking how God can still find fault, and answers with this question, borrowing the prophets' image of potter and clay. Calvinist readers often see individual predestination here; others see Paul describing God's dealings with whole peoples.

posts.display: “The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart,” that is, the word of faith we are proclaiming: that if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved.
posts.caption: Paul's point is that God's message is not far off or hard to reach: it is as near as one's own mouth and heart, and anyone who confesses Jesus as Lord and believes God raised him will be saved. He borrows Moses' words from Deuteronomy 30:14. "Jesus is Lord" is thought to be one of the earliest Christian confessions of faith. In the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, "Lord" (kyrios) often stood in for God's own name.

Paul has just pictured God's people as an olive tree rooted in Israel, with non-Jewish believers grafted in like wild shoots, and warned them not to look down on the Jewish people. This line is why, in his view, Israel remains loved by God. In 1965 the Catholic Church cited it in Nostra Aetate, the landmark declaration that reshaped Catholic–Jewish relations.

After three chapters on God's plan for Israel and the nations, Paul breaks into praise. The next lines draw on Isaiah and Job, and this short hymn closes the long, closely argued first part of the letter. From the next chapter on, Paul turns to everyday life: how believers treat one another and the world around them.

With "therefore," Paul turns from explaining his message to describing how to live it. His readers knew animal sacrifice from temples, both the Jewish temple in Jerusalem and Rome's many shrines; Paul speaks instead of offering one's whole self. The Greek behind "spiritual service of worship," logike latreia, can also be translated "reasonable service," as in the King James Version.

Paul's point is that believers shouldn't let the surrounding world press them into its mold, but be changed from the inside, starting with how they think. "Conformed" means pressed into the shape of a pattern, while "transformed" translates the Greek metamorphoo, the root of the English word metamorphosis. Matthew and Mark use the same verb for Jesus' transfiguration. A renewed mind, Paul says, learns to recognize what God wants.

The last line of a chapter full of short sayings about living with others, such as "weep with those who weep" and "bless those who persecute you," which echoes Jesus' own teaching. The point is that answering evil with evil lets evil win; good is the stronger response. Just before this, Paul quotes Proverbs on feeding a hungry enemy, which will "heap burning coals on his head," an image whose exact meaning is still debated.

Paul sums up the commandments in one line from Leviticus 19:18: love your neighbor as yourself. His reasoning: real love never harms anyone, so it fulfills everything the law is aiming at, much as Jesus summarized the law. The chapter opens with a passage telling believers to submit to the governing authorities and pay taxes, written while Nero was emperor and read in very different ways through history.

The believers in Rome were divided over food and holy days: some ate only vegetables, others ate anything; some honored special days, others treated every day alike. Many scholars think the tension was partly between Jewish and non-Jewish believers. Paul asks both sides not to judge each other, and this verse is his reason. The words are used in many Christian funeral services.

A prayer that closes the main body of the letter: Paul asks the "God of hope" to fill the believers in Rome with joy and peace, so that their hope overflows. Hope runs through the whole letter, and here Paul presents it as a gift of the Holy Spirit. He then shares his plans: Jerusalem first, then Rome, then Spain. Acts tells how he did reach Rome, but as a prisoner; whether he ever reached Spain is unknown.

The last chapter commends Phoebe, whom many scholars think carried this letter to Rome, and greets about two dozen people by name, several of them women. Near the end Paul warns against those who stir up divisions, then adds this: he rejoices that their obedience is known everywhere, and wants them wise about good and innocent of evil. It recalls Jesus' words in Matthew 10: "as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves."

As he closes, Paul promises that the God of peace will soon defeat evil, picturing Satan crushed underfoot, an image that seems to echo Genesis 3:15, where the serpent's head is to be crushed. After this blessing, the scribe who wrote the letter down adds his own greeting: "I, Tertius." The letter then ends with praise "to the only wise God." That's Romans. Thank you for reading it with me.
